Plant the Moon Challenge
Brown Space Engineering – Team 2
Team Number: 13128
Undergraduate Challenge
4/21/2023

Introduction
With the development of the Artemis program and other long duration human spaceflight
missions, it is becoming increasingly clear that implementing a renewable food source will be a
critical challenge to overcome. Since the beginning of human history, agriculture and food
propagation have been central to the development of our species, and as we expand to the Moon
and beyond, the same will be the case. Forgetting the large variation in temperature, lack of
atmospheric oxygen, minimal to no ground water, and intense incident radiation, the soil which
covers the surface of the Moon is desolate and lacks the nutrients necessary to sustain any life.
That being said, there are plants that can flourish in nutrient-poor environments on Earth. We aim
to investigate those properties of cacti, one of Earth’s most survivable plants, and determine
whether they can succeed with lunar regolith as a replacement for Earth sand. We chose to use
the Opuntia cactus because of its ability to produce fruit, flourish without significant nutrients,
and propagate. Propagation is the process by which cacti and other succulents can grow from
cuttings. This process can lead to higher crop success rates, which is a positive for extraterrestrial
growth. Its ability to propagate also poses an interesting scientific challenge to explore.
While it is known that cacti are able to survive in arid and nutrient-poor soil, there has
never been an analysis of cactus growth completed in Lunar regolith.With this experiment, we
aim to begin to lay the foundation of this work. Our goal was to test if Opuntia cactus
propagation in lunar highland simulant is affected by different soil and nutrient conditions. We
compared cactus growth in a ratio of 55% Lunar simulant and soil mixture by volume to
Opuntia’s ideal growth environment, the same volumetric ratio of sand and soil. Additionally, we
tested the effectiveness of cactus fertilizer for increasing growth. We aim to show that cactus
propagation in lunar soil is first possible, before attempting to tackle other goals which might

have an effect on optimizing other species' growth. In order to best prepare us for the reality of
crop propagation, it is important to investigate all types of crops, both the traditional and the odd.
Theory
An interesting trait of succulents like cacti is their ability to reproduce both sexually via
the creation of seeds and asexually through propagation. Propagation is the ability to asexually
grow new cactus plants by planting the cutting of a mature cactus plant in ideal soil conditions.
Past research has shown that a cacti population can be healthily grown and multiplied via this
method (Finiti et al, 2013). Cactus plants ideally grow in a sandy loam, a type of soil composed
of silt, sand, and clay. As sand and lunar regolith are similar in particulate matter size (Savio,
1989), we came to the conclusion it could serve as a replacement for sand in a loam like soil
mixture. This conclusion has also been proven in the research environment, with Carrier et. al.
showing that regolith can be a replacement for sand in a sandy soil mixture (Carrier, 2003).
Since cacti grow in a loam environment, and regolith has shown to be a viable
replacement for sand in loam, we chose a cactus species as our test crop. However, to the best of
our knowledge, no research has shown that cacti can reproduce through propagation in lunar
regolith. The Opuntia genus has been shown to have success in a regolith environment with
Opuntia ficus-indica (Barbary fig cactus) been seen to germinate in lunar regolith with the help
of Endomycorrhizal Fungi (Konings-Dudin, 2014), which gave even more reason to pick a
cactus from this genus. For this study, we chose to use the Cactaceae Opuntia (Prickly Pear), for
its ability to grow in a low-nutrient environment, reproduce via propagation, and ability to
produce an edible fruit (Savio, 1989). Opuntia cactus fruit has been successfully used in

medicine as anti-inflammatory agents, and even to treat Type 2 Diabetes (Ahmed 2005). In
addition to producing fruit, Opuntia are extremely drought-resistant.
We designed this experiment to test the variability of success that Opuntia cacti would
have when grown in a lunar regolith environment. Due to the similarities between the standard
growth condition preferences of the prickly pear cactus and the conditions we fabricated for our
experiment, we posit that the addition of an earth soil mix will speed up the growth process of
these species. We predict the biomass of our samples to increase by different extents depending
on the makeup of their growth substrate. We predict that the Opuntia will grow the best in the
loam environment, as that is the natural and ideal environment. We expect the cacti in the
regolith to grow, but to a lesser extent than the cacti in loam.
Research has shown that the usage of fertilizer in the growth process increases the
nutritive value of these plants (Gonzalez et al., 2018). Therefore, we decided to add separate
groups of cacti that would be treated with fertilizer in both the regolith simulant and regular soil
conditions of our experiment design. We predicted that the overall growth of plants would be
higher in the fertilizer group than in the group cacti without fertilizer.
Measurement Methods
Our experimental setup consisted of 20 plants harvested in Southern California and
shipped to Providence. 10 of the pots contained our “Ideal Soil” mixture which will be composed
of 55% sand and 45% soil. The others consisted of a mixture of 55% regular soil and 45% lunar
simulant. We split the group of regolith mixed with soil in two: one half having no additional
nutrients, and one with a cactus fertilizer. We left the remaining 5 regolith-filled and 5 soil-filled
pots unaltered. The plants receiving additional nutrients were treated twice a month, with 5

milliliters of liquid fertilizer per plant. At the end of the growing period of 8 weeks, we uprooted
our samples and took quantitative measurements of root growth and plant weight changes.
Overall, not many measurements were needed since the only definitive goal was to get
the cactus to successfully grow in a regolith soil composition. Before planting, we we measured
the initial height and weight of each sample. The heights would provide an easy visual
representation of growth, and the weight difference would prove whether or not the cactus had
absorbed water, proving that the cacti weren’t necessarily dead, and had the potential to grow
given more time even if no visual growth was present. The weights were measured using a
standard scale, and the heights were measured by taking photos on a blank background with
rulers along the side as a reference.
Plant growth occurred in one of Brown’s Plant Environmental Center Greenhouses,
which was operating under their standard lighting and temperature protocols in order to optimize
plant growth. Lighting was controlled using full spectrum growth lights, and the temperature was
controlled using their system of fans and heating and cooling to keep ambient temperature
between 68 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit, with moderate humidity of 30 - 40 percent.

During the planting process, to perfect the ratios of regolith to earth soil, ideally
mimicking the soil-to-sand ratio cacti grow in, we ran density calculations of both to solve for
the volumes to use in each pot. The soil which was used was ProMix HP Mycorrhizae High
Porosity soil and sand, both provided by Brown’s research greenhouse. After planting, the cacti
were watered to field capacity and left to begin the rooting process. Wooden stakes were added
to support cacti and were left in the potted plants until they were uprooted.
For the first three weeks, the plants were watered once per week, following the guidelines
we found for general cactus transplanting. However, due to the visible dehydration in the cactus,
this was changed after 3 weeks. During the first three weeks of growth is where we saw the most
death in our plants. From the fourth week onward, plants were watered twice per week for the
remainder of the experiment. After making the change to twice per week watering, we saw much
less plant death and poor health. The reason for the dehydration is not exactly known, but we
imagine the cross country travel, transplantation process, and small soil volume in each pot were
factors that lead to increased evaporation.
Starting on March 10th, we began fertilizing cactus plants, providing each plant in those
experimental groups with 5mL of Cute Farms Succulent, Cacti, and Aloe Fertilizer. This
fertilizer contained nitrogen in the form of Ammonia and Nitrate Nitrogen. Fertilizer also
contained available phosphorus in the form of Phosphoric Acid, as well as potassium in the form
of soluble Potash.
During the growth phase, we collected the pH of each soil pod once per ounce after they
were watered. We saw no variation in soil pH throughout the entire experiment. At the end of the
growth period, plants were uprooted and the soil mixture was removed from the soil. Plants were
then weighed and measured using the same setup as the initial measurements.

Results
In all groups, growth was observed. Phylloclades that start out larger grew more over the
course of the growth period than those that started out smaller. To correct for the randomness in
initial size, percent difference in weight was used to measure growth. As seen in Table 1, group 1
showed the highest growth on average, followed by group 4, group 2, and finally group 3.
Within each group, there were multiple deaths. Each death occurred early on, but the
dead cacti remained in the experiment. These dead cacti lost weight over time as they decayed
and ended with less weight than they started with. Due to this, their percent differences were
negative. This impacts the values shown in Table 3 (as a negative value pulls down the average
even more than a zero value would). Each group, except group 3, had 1 death. Group 3 had 2
deaths.

Figure 1 displays the full distribution of percent difference in weight. Those that died can
be seen far below the other data points. Those that flowered are represented by a green data
point. In both the sand-soil and regolith-soil groups, one cacti flowered while in both of the
fertilized groups, two cacti flowered.
Analysis
The first variable in our experiment was lunar regolith versus soil without fertilizer. Our
experiment demonstrates the viability of cacti growth in our regolith mixture without fertilizer,
though a larger sample size in the future could give us more concrete information on growth
conditions in soil versus lunar regolith. Both the regolith mixture and soil groups without

fertilizer had one flowering plant. While the soil group had one cacti death, the regolith group
had two. Although the growth rate of plants in simulant was significantly lower than those in the
soil and sand mixture, the plants in simulant still had a positive growth rate. Given the small
sample size of our experiment, these results reflect comparable success across soil and regolith
without fertilizer. As seen in Figure 1, the growth of plants in this regolith mixture group, Group
3, had much more variation in percentage weight difference and a slightly lower average growth
than that of Group 1, the soil control. Though soil provides more reliable growth conditions,
Lunar regolith is certainly viable for Opuntia Cactus growth.
Fertilizer proved to be an effective way to increase cacti growth. Relative to the growth
rate in the simulant without fertilizer, fertilized cacti in the simulant experienced nearly 6%
higher growth on average. Furthermore, an additional cactus flowered in Group 4—regolith
mixture and fertilizer—and one fewer died than those in Group 3—regolith without fertilizer.
Fertilized cacti appeared to grow in a regolith mixture nearly if not as effectively as they did in a
soil-sand mixture. Their average percent growth was slightly higher (9.3% relative to 7.1%) than
Group 2 and the same number of cacti flowered and died in both Groups 2 and 4. These results
tentatively indicate that cactus fertilizer is an effective way to boost cactus growth in lunar
simulants.
While our experiment demonstrates the potential for prickly pear growth in simulant,
increasing the sample size could dramatically deepen experimental findings. A two-way analysis
of variance (ANOVA) was used to measure the impact of our two experimental factors. The
result was that neither factor (regolith and fertilizer) had a statistically significant impact on
growth of the cacti. This is most likely due to the low sample size of our experiment. It is
difficult to find a statistically significant result with low power.

While the solid growth rates in cacti could indicate that cacti can be effectively grown in
lunar regolith, it may also indicate that the simulant we used, Exolith Lab’s LHS-1, did not
effectively model the conditions that might inhibit plant growth in lunar soil. While germination
rates for simulant and true regolith were both nearly 100% in Paul et. al. 2022, their JSC-1A
simulant controls demonstrated significantly stronger root growth and survivability than the
Apollo soil counterparts (4). Just like we cannot completely separate the cacti’s success from
experimental constraints, cacti deaths may be partially due to them as well. The fact that cacti
died across all four groups indicates the challenge of propagating phylloclades, especially in light
of the extended period of time that cacti spent out of the soil while traveling from California and
lack of watering in the early weeks of the project.
Conclusion
Our experiment demonstrated that Opuntia cuttings can be successfully propagated in a
majority Lunar regolith soil environment. We saw phylloclade growth, including bud and flower
development, on plants in all groups, including both experimental groups. While the plants
grown in Opuntia’s ideal environment without fertilizer grew more than the corresponding
regolith group, samples in both experimental groups showed growth from the beginning of the
experiment. Additionally, plants in both the ideal soil and regolith groups showed bud and flower
development, an indication of good plant health. There was plant death, but this is most likely
attributable to issues with watering within the first weeks of the experiment as we saw no plant
death after the watering schedule was changed.
While the initial goal of our work was achieved, there are limitations to our work. These
come mostly from the small sample size and issues with watering at the beginning stage of the

growth period. Put simply, 20 plants are not enough to gather statistically significant data on
plant growth as there is too much plant-to-plant variation for trends to establish themselves.
Additionally, the issues that we encountered with watering within the first weeks could have had
an effect on the overall results. Death, or stress that the cacti were under during the first few
weeks of the growth period, could have had effects on the overall growth of the plants
throughout the entire experiment. Because of a limited supply of Opuntia phylloclades, we were
unable to replant cacti that died during this period. Other uncertainties come from aspects of our
experimental design. Since our goal was a proof of concept, we did not set up systems to
measure every aspect of plant growth, nor did we complete advanced plant health analysis. Our
results show that cacti can survive, and even grow, in a majority lunar regolith soil environment.
This discovery allows for further research questions to be investigated.
With a higher sample size, a more detailed set of analysis procedures could be performed.
While Paul et. al. 2022 performs a thorough analysis of the comparison between the growth of
Arabidopsis Thaliana in lunar regolith and simulant, their experiments could be extended by
performing a similar procedure comparing simulant to soil. An experiment like this one, in
comparison to Paul et. al. 2022, could help determine the efficacy of simulant as an
environmental model for plant growth in Arabidopsis Thaliana or other plants like those of the
opuntia genus. While our experiment demonstrates the capacity for cacti to be grown in simulant,
testing a variety of regolith to soil ratios in both mare and highland simulants could determine
the minimum soil required to optimize cactus growth. While typical NDVI analysis is not
effective on cacti, the health of samples could still be computed spectroscopically by performing
spectral measurements in the near infrared and calculating the cacti indexes discussed in
Hartfield et al., 2022.

While imperfect, the growth of cactus even in regolith and additional conditions of
distress demonstrates the potential role Opuntia cacti could play in space exploration and
discovery. We for one cannot wait to eat some prickly pear grown fresh on the Moon.
